edition.notes: The Longmans reprint digitised by Google and redistributed by the Internet Archive as item TheMassAStudyOf, whose bibliographic record gives the date as 1922. The first edition appeared in 1912; the reprint's pagination is the one used for every locus registered here and was checked directly against the scan. Fortescue died in 1923, so this printing carries no revision by a later hand. His own footnotes preserve the disagreements among Probst, Baumstark, Drews, Duchesne, Bona, Gihr, and others, and those disagreements are part of what this edition witnesses.

passages.context: Chapter IV opening, printed p. 172: Gregory the Great 'left the Roman liturgy practically in the state in which we still have it', with three changes named (Kyrie eleison, the addition to the Hanc igitur, the insertion of the Pater noster before the Communion), the 'constant tradition that St. Gregory was the last to touch the essential part of the Mass, namely the Canon', and Benedict XIV's dictum quoted in the footnote from De ss. Missae Sacrificio II, xii, 12.

passages.context: Printed p. 227 on the prayers at the foot of the altar: 'That all this is rather preparation than part of the Mass itself is shown by its recital at the foot of the altar, before the celebrant goes up to it', followed by the medieval variants (Salisbury, Dominican, Carthusian, Carmelite, Lyons) and the Apologiae of the ninth and tenth centuries, which Fortescue calls 'certainly Gallican (Northern) in origin' on the following page. A footnote records that Aufer a nobis and Oramus te were said in the medieval rite of the papal chapel, where the words sancta sanctorum and quorum reliquiae hic sunt had a particular local aptness.

passages.context: Printed p. 232 on the origin of the Kyrie: the middle of the fourth century as the date of its first certain appearance; Chrysostom quotes it; Etheria heard it at Jerusalem and translates it, 'et diacono dicente singulorum nomina semper pisinni plurimi stant respondentes semper: kyrie eleyson, quod dicimus nos: miserere Domine'; 'This is exactly the Antiochene litany with the answer to each clause. From Antioch the use of such litanies spread throughout the East. They and their answer: Kyrie eleison occur constantly in all Eastern liturgies, most often of all in the Antiochene-Byzantine family.' A footnote records that the Kyrie occurs twelve times in the liturgy of St James and three in St Mark, that its normal place is the answer to a litany, and that it is translated in every non-Greek rite except the Coptic.

passages.context: Printed pp. 234-235 on the Roman Kyrie. Gregory the Great's letter to John of Syracuse is quoted: 'We neither say nor have said Kyrie eleison as it is said by the Greeks ... But in the daily Masses we leave out some things which are generally said; we only say Kyrie eleison and Christe eleison, that we should dwell rather longer on these words of prayer.' Fortescue notes that the letter mentions 'what is the unique speciality of the Roman rite, the formula: Christe eleison', that in all Eastern liturgies they say only Kyrie eleison, and that John the Deacon's ascription of the Kyrie's introduction to Gregory is contradicted by the Council of Vaison, which shows it older. Page 235 continues that at Antioch the Kyrie answers the five petitions of the deacon's Synapte and that in all Eastern liturgies it occurs in this way; that in the Gelasian Sacramentary's Ordination Mass the rubric is 'Et post modicum intervallum mox incipiant omnes Kyrie eleison cum litania'; that down to the ninth century there was at Rome, on days that had no Gloria, a litany at this place; and that 'on two days in the year, the eves of Easter and Whitsunday, our Mass still begins with a litany, in which the Kyrie fits naturally. The ordination Mass still has the litany, as in the Gelasian book.'
passages.notes: Read visually in the page images. Artifact pages 254-255 carry printed pp. 234-235. Fortescue's reconstruction is an identified early twentieth-century scholarly account and is cited as such; the ascription to Gregory of the Kyrie's introduction is one he expressly rejects.

passages.context: Printed p. 288 on the introduction of the Creed into the Roman Mass: Berno of Reichenau reports what he saw in 1014, when Henry II noticed that no creed was sung at his coronation on 14 February 1014 and Benedict VIII eventually ordered it sung after the Gospel at Rome. Fortescue records that most authors accept the story and date the Creed at Rome from 1014, and names in the footnote those who do not (Probst, Mabillon, Thalhofer, Martene), together with the observation that the Creed's restriction to Sundays and feasts is 'still a sign that it is not an essential element'.

passages.context: Printed p. 305 on the offertory prayers: they are medieval, appear at Rome only in the fourteenth century, seem to fill the void left by the disappearance of the old offering by the faithful, and 'The Offertory prayers adopted by the revisors of 1570 are those in the XIVth Roman Ordo. All are taken or adapted from various, mostly non-Roman sources.' Suscipe sancte Pater 'occurs first (with slight variations) in the prayerbook of Charles the Bald (875-877)', and hanc immaculatam hostiam is called 'an anticipation of the consecration, a dramatic misplacement'. The mixed chalice is traced to Justin, Irenaeus and the epitaph of Abercius.
passages.notes: Read visually in the page image. The preceding page, printed p. 304, carries Micrologus's statement that the Roman order had no prayer between the offering and the Secret; that sentence was read in the optical text only and is not relied on here.

passages.context: Printed p. 387 on the Agnus Dei: it 'was added to fill up the time of the fraction'; the Liber Pontificalis says Sergius I (687-701) ordered it sung by clergy and people at the breaking of the Lord's body; it was at first sung once, twice in the eleventh century, and John Beleth in the twelfth describes the present threefold form with Dona nobis pacem, while Innocent III notes churches, the Lateran among them, that kept miserere nobis three times.

passages.context: Printed p. 394 on the last Gospel: throughout the middle ages it belonged to the priest's thanksgiving and 'was in no wise an element of the Mass'; the Sarum Missal has it said on the way back to the sacristy; Burchard's ceremonial of 1502 allows it at the altar; and 'Pius V in his reformed missal (1570) for the first time admits it as part of the Mass'. Fortescue adds that it is not sung by the deacon, has no solemnities at High Mass, and is said by a bishop on his way from the altar.

work.author: Adrian Fortescue (1874-1923)
work.description: Adrian Fortescue's historical study of the Roman Mass, first published in 1912. It reconstructs the development of the Roman rite from the earliest witnesses to the Missal of Pius V and then walks the Order of Mass unit by unit, naming its sources, its earliest secure attestations, and the points at which the evidence is disputed. It is an identified early twentieth-century scholarly reconstruction, not a magisterial or official source, and its conclusions are cited here as such. Loci are printed page numbers.
work.title: The Mass: A Study of the Roman Liturgy
